note.text:
Peaceful coexistence means people who are different (in religion, language, tribe or culture) living together without violence and with respect.
Its advantages: people feel safe, children go to school, trade grows, and the community works together.
In the talk, Christians and Muslims, Anglophones and Francophones share the same market, school and water point. When two families quarrelled about a fence, the quarter head helped them talk; they apologised and shared the cost.
Useful phrases:
• Disagreeing politely: “I see your point, but …” “I'm afraid I don't agree.”
• Apologising: “I'm sorry. It was my fault.” Accepting: “That's all right.”
• Solving a problem: “Let's talk about it calmly.” “Why don't we share it?”

worked_example.problem: {n} and {m} both want the same seat in class. Write what they can say to solve the problem peacefully.
steps: {n} disagrees politely: “I see your point, but I sat here first.”
{m} suggests a solution: “Why don't we take turns? You today, me tomorrow.”
They agree and apologise: “That's fair. Sorry I shouted.” — “That's all right.”
worked_example.answer: They speak calmly, disagree politely, suggest taking turns and apologise.

cards.idea: Read this short talk. (In class you would listen to it.)
example: In our quarter live Christians and Muslims, Anglophones and Francophones, and people from many tribes. We speak different languages at home, but we share the same market, school and water point.
Living together in peace means respecting other people's beliefs and customs, even when they are different from ours. When we disagree, we talk calmly and listen to each other.
Last year two families quarrelled about a fence. The quarter head invited them to talk. Each family explained, they apologised to each other, and they agreed to share the cost of a new fence.
